question: A 55-year-old construction worker falls off a 2-story scaffolding and injures his back. His coworkers bring him to the urgent care clinic within 30 minutes of the fall. He complains of left lower-limb weakness and loss of sensation in the right lower limb. He does not have any past medical history. His vital signs are stable. A neurologic examination reveals a total loss of motor function when testing left knee extension, along with the left-sided loss of light touch sensation from the mid-thigh and below. There is a right-sided loss of pin-prick sensation of the lateral leg and entire foot. At this time of acute injury, what other finding is most likely to be found in this patient?

options.opa: Left-sided numbness at the level of the lesion
options.opd: Right-sided loss of proprioception and vibration sensation
options.ope: Left-sided spastic paralysis below the lesion

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Fall from height" -> "Back injury" -> "Spinal cord injury" -> "Hemisection of spinal cord" -> "Brown-Séquard syndrome" -> "Ipsilateral motor loss below lesion" -> "Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation" -> "Left-sided spastic paralysis below the lesion" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Fall from height" -> "Back injury" -> "Spinal cord injury" -> "Hemisection of spinal cord" -> "Brown-Séquard syndrome" -> "Ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration" -> "Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation" -> "Right-sided loss of proprioception and vibration sensation" -> 60%

CHAIN: "Fall from height" -> "Back injury" -> "Spinal cord injury" -> "Hemisection of spinal cord" -> "Brown-Séquard syndrome" -> "Ipsilateral loss of sensation at level of lesion" -> "Left-sided numbness at the level of the lesion" -> 70%

CHAIN: "Fall from height" -> "Back injury" -> "Spinal cord injury" -> "Hemisection of spinal cord" -> "Brown-Séquard syndrome" -> "Ipsilateral motor loss below lesion" -> "Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation" -> "Left-sided extensor plantar response" -> 75%

CHAIN: "Fall from height" -> "Back injury" -> "Spinal cord injury" -> "Hemisection of spinal cord" -> "Brown-Séquard syndrome" -> "Intact sacral reflexes" -> "Intact voluntary anal contraction" -> 65%
enhanced_information: In a patient with a spinal cord injury at the thoracic level following a fall, the most likely finding would be left-sided numbness at the level of the lesion. Autonomic dysreflexia, which can occur in spinal cord injuries, may lead to hypertension and bradycardia.
analysis: The clinical presentation is suggestive of Brown-Séquard syndrome, which is characterized by ipsilateral motor loss and loss of proprioception and vibration sensation, along with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation. In this case, the patient has left-sided motor loss and right-sided loss of pin-prick sensation, consistent with this syndrome. In the acute phase of spinal cord injury, flaccid paralysis is more common due to spinal shock, rather than spastic paralysis. Therefore, left-sided spastic paralysis below the lesion is unlikely at this stage.
